                               RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                        CASE NO. 3:25-CV-05377-WHO
               Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO           Document 30       Filed 09/30/25       Page 2 of 10



1
              Defendant United Wholesale Mortgage, LLC (“United” or “Defendant”) filed a motion
2
     seeking a stay of discovery based on a motion to dismiss it had not yet filed. D.E. 28. A stay is not
3
     justified. The Court has wide discretion on a motion like this, but there is no cause to invoke it
4
     here. United rests its request simply on the cost of litigation, a wholly insufficient basis upon which
5
     to grant relief.
6
                                        FACTUAL BACKGROUND
7
              This case is in its infancy. Plaintiffs filed their complaint on June 26, 2025. D.E. 1. The
8
     parties entered an agreed briefing schedule, and on August 22, 2025, United filed a motion to
9

10
     dismiss. D.E. 21. On September 12, 2025, consistent with Fed. R. Civ. P. 15, Plaintiffs amended

11   their complaint. D.E. 26. Four days later, on September 16, 2025, United filed the instant Motion

12   to Stay Discovery. D.E. 28. United filed its renewed motion to dismiss on September 26, 2025.

13   D.E. 29.

14                                               ARGUMENT

15            United requests what big companies always request in cases like this – a free pass from the
16   normal rules of discovery and litigation. Such stays are disfavored, and there is no cause to grant
17   one here. United bases its request on two things: first, that its latest and greatest motion to dismiss
18   is likely to succeed, and second, that discovery costs money. This is a complex case involving a
19   number of different alternative claims addressing the same conduct, and a preliminary peek at
20   United’s motion to dismiss should telegraph to the Court that there are complex, weedy issues here
21
     that are not appropriate for resolution on a Rule 12 motion to dismiss. Thus, it is far too early to
22
     endow United with the benefits arising from the grant of a dispositive motion that is not even
23
     briefed. Second, courts have said that cost is not a sufficient basis to give a party a stay of
24
     discovery. Every defendant thinks its motion to dismiss will succeed, and thus that is not grounds
25
     to delay the case. A stay is not justified here.
26
         I.      Motions to Stay Discovery When a Dispositive Motion is Pending.
27
              The Ninth Circuit has developed a vast body of caselaw regarding stays of discovery when
28
     a motion to dismiss is filed. Indeed, United’s motion to stay is replete with citations to legions of

                                                2
                                  RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                           CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
            Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO              Document 30        Filed 09/30/25     Page 3 of 10



1
     unpublished decisions on this issue. A return to basic principles is helpful in these circumstances.
2
     Discovery may only be stayed for good cause. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(1). Of course, “[h]ad the
3
     Federal Rules contemplated that a motion to dismiss under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6) would stay
4
     discovery, the Rules would contain a provision to that effect.” Gray v. First Winthrop Corp., 133
5
     F.R.D. 39, 40 (N.D. Cal. 1990); Skellerup Indus. Ltd. v. City of Los Angeles, 163 F.R.D. 598, 601
6
     (C.D. Cal. 1995) (same rule). They contain no such provision. In general, the decision of whether
7
     to stay discovery is discretionary, and good cause exists to stay discovery when the district court
8
     is convinced a plaintiff’s complaint will not survive Rule 12 review. Flynn v. Nevada, 345 F.R.D.
9

10
     338, 343 (D. Nev. 2024). Motions to stay discovery are generally disfavored. See, e.g., White v. E-

11   Loan, Inc., No. C 05-02080 SI, 2006 WL 2850041, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 5, 2006); see also

12   Washington v. United States Dep’t of Homeland Sec., No. 4:19-CV-5210-RMP, 2020 WL

13   4667545, at *2 (E.D. Wash. June 4, 2020) (“Blanket stays of discovery pending resolution of a

14   dispositive motion generally are disfavored in this Circuit.”).

15             A party seeking a stay bears a “heavy burden” of making a strong showing of why
16   discovery should be denied. SVB Fin. Grp. v. Fed. Deposit Ins. Corp., No. 23-CV-06543-BLF,
17   2024 WL 1898439, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 29, 2024). This is akin to a double hurdle of making a
18   “strong” showing to meet a “heavy” burden. In this District, discovery proceeds after a case
19   management conference. See Local Rule 16-7. There is no reason here to depart from that standard
20   procedure. “[A]ll defendants believe that their motions to dismiss are meritorious, and if that was
21
     the standard, discovery would be stayed in all cases where motions to dismiss are filed.” Cortazar
22
     v. CA Ventures LLC, No. 1:19-CV-22075-UU, 2019 WL 13092851, at *1 (S.D. Fla. July 30, 2019)
23
     (quoting Eisenband v. Starion Energy, Inc., No. 17-cv-80195-KAM, D.E. 38 (S.D. Fla. June 16,
24
     2017)).
25
               As noted in Defendant’s Motion, this District generally applies a two-part test to determine
26
     whether to stay discovery after a motion to dismiss is filed. The motion must be dispositive of the
27
     whole case, and second, the court must decide whether the pending dispositive motion can be
28


                                                 3
                                   RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                            CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
               Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO          Document 30        Filed 09/30/25      Page 4 of 10



1
     decided absent additional discovery. Pac. Lumber Co. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh,
2
     PA, 220 F.R.D. 349, 352 (N.D. Cal. 2003) (noting both elements are required). And even then, if
3
     both factors are satisfied, the court need not issue a protective order under Rule 26. Hoopes
4
     Vineyard LLC v. Cnty. of Napa, No. 24-CV-06256-CRB, 2025 WL 41929, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Jan.
5
     6, 2025) (“The presence of these two factors permits, but does not require, the court to stay
6
     discovery until the pending motion is resolved.”) (emphasis added). The first factor is most
7
     relevant here – United’s motion is not dispositive. The second factor is less dispositive here
8
     because Plaintiffs agree no further discovery is necessary to deny the instant motions. However,
9

10
     discovery would help to confirm the existence and operation of all third-party trackers on the

11   website, including server to server tracking that cannot be reviewed without access to internal

12   documents. See D.E. 26 at ¶¶ 34, 35. Motions to stay are disfavored for good reason. United has

13   done no more than copy and paste its motion to dismiss into this motion to stay and make general,

14   vague references to cost and burden. That does not constitute good cause.

15      II.      United’s Motion to Dismiss
16            United spends most of its motion regurgitating its theories on its initial motion to dismiss,
17   claiming that its arguments will certainly, assuredly dispose of this entire case. United also claims
18   that this Court should review its arguments asserted in its prior motion to dismiss, since it only
19   filed a new one a few days ago. D.E. 29. For the proposition that the Court can look to a previously
20   filed motion to dismiss (that is essentially moot), United cites In re Google Digital Advert.
21
     Antitrust Litig., No. 20-CV-03556-BLF, 2020 WL 7227159, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 8, 2020). But
22
     in that case (an antitrust matter, unlike here), Plaintiffs had already essentially conceded that the
23
     motion to dismiss was likely to succeed: “Google’s motion to dismiss presents formidable
24
     arguments, which could prove difficult for Plaintiffs to overcome, even considering that leave to
25
     amend is freely given…Plaintiffs do not appear to contest this conclusion.” Id. Plaintiffs make no
26
     such concession here and have not even responded to United’s forthcoming motion to dismiss yet.
27
     Pointing to a moot motion to dismiss is not sufficient on a motion to stay discovery like this one,
28


                                                4
                                  RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                           CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
            Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO            Document 30        Filed 09/30/25       Page 5 of 10



1
     and the fact that United filed this motion to stay without having filed its renewed motion to dismiss
2
     demonstrates that United is putting the cart before the horse.
3
            And consider what United is really asking for: for the Court to look at a motion that is now
4
     moot to justify relief in the new motion it presents here, because its days-ago filed non-moot
5
     motion will surely succeed. That is attenuated and wrong. This case presents complex issues of
6
     contract formation, tort law, and tracking and privacy law. Pixel cases nationwide are complex and
7
     different district courts often dismiss some claims but not others in distinct ways that vary by
8
     district, by judge, and by Circuit. Compare, e.g., Shah v. Cap. One Fin. Corp., 768 F. Supp. 3d
9

10
     1033 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (denying motion to dismiss in part in pixel case), with Smith v. Loyola Univ.

11   Med. Ctr., No. 23 CV 15828, 2024 WL 3338941 (N.D. Ill. July 9, 2024) (similar in a medical pixel

12   case). This Court need not delve into the vast number of pixel cases to satisfy itself that these

13   allegations raise complex issues. Handing United a victory like staying discovery is not justified.

14          Further, the discovery that Plaintiffs plan to propound here is narrowly tailored to this case.

15   Plaintiffs will request any document associated with their own use of Defendant’s website,
16   documents associated with how Defendant shared information with third parties, and technical
17   information showing how Defendant’s website employed the technologies laid out in the
18   complaint. This is not a fishing expedition into every last aspect of Defendant’s comings and
19   goings in the mortgage market. This case is about online data collection and how United harvests,
20   collects, processes, and sells certain kinds of data from consumers. It is not an antitrust challenge
21
     to an entire line of business of a giant company like Google that could implicate millions of intra-
22
     company communications.
23
            And in general, complex cases like this one are not suited for abbreviated briefing in this
24
     forum on a motion to stay discovery. Hoopes Vineyard LLC, 2025 WL 41929, at *1 (“The parties
25
     spend significant time debating the likely merits of Napa County’s as-yet unfiled motion to dismiss
26
     Plaintiffs’ first amended complaint. But Plaintiffs’ allegations and Napa County’s potential
27
     defenses are complex and not suited for abbreviated briefing in a motion to stay.”). The district
28


                                               5
                                 RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                          CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
            Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO             Document 30        Filed 09/30/25      Page 6 of 10



1
     court must be “convinced that the plaintiff will be unable to state a claim for relief.” Wenger v.
2
     Monroe, 282 F.3d 1068, 1077 (9th Cir. 2002), (quoting Wood v. McEwen, 644 F.2d 797, 801 (9th
3
     Cir. 1981)) (emphasis added). Plaintiffs need not respond to United’s cribbed arguments from its
4
     motion to dismiss in this motion. But for example, United repeatedly invokes a “consent” defense.
5
     D.E. 28 at 10, 12. Generally speaking, consent questions (like scope) are ill suited for resolution
6
     at the motion to dismiss stage. See, e.g., Zarif v. Hwareh.com, Inc., No. 23-CV-0565-BAS-DEB,
7
     __ F.Supp.3d __, 2025 WL 486317, at *6 (S.D. Cal. Feb. 13, 2025); see also Planned Parenthood
8
     Fed’n of Am., Inc. v. Ctr. for Med. Progress, 735 F. App’x 241, 247 (9th Cir. 2018); Balanzar v.
9

10
     Fid. Brokerage Servs., LLC, 654 F. Supp. 3d 1075, 1081 (S.D. Cal. 2023). And Plaintiffs allege in

11   the very first paragraph of their complaint that they did not consent to the collection here. D.E. 26

12   at ¶¶ 1, 71, 82, 109. All these issues can (and should) be briefed more fulsomely in the normal

13   course. United is not entitled to a full-blown response to its motion to dismiss for Plaintiffs to

14   avoid the grant of this motion.

15          United’s Motion is light on what matters most here: some indication of why discovery will
16   harm it, or why discovery is not appropriate in this case. United is essentially asking the Court for
17   a Mulligan on participating in litigation in the normal course in federal court, and can come up
18   with no justification more immediate than litigation costs. For example, United asserts that limiting
19   discovery will “promote efficiency and reduce the burden on UWM and the Court[.]” D.E. 28 at
20   6. United later asserts that requiring discovery will be “costly” and a “substantial waste of
21
     resources.” D.E. 28 at 7. A stay is not justified just because discovery may cost money. See, e.g.,
22
     Hoopes Vineyard LLC, 2025 WL 41929, at *1 (“Moreover, Napa County fails to identify a
23
     particular or specific need for a protective order, asserting only that a stay will promote efficiency
24
     for the Court and the parties and conserve the parties’ resources. Such blanket concerns, which are
25
     true in the mine run of litigation, do not establish good cause for a protective order.”); Smith v.
26
     Levine Leichtman Cap. Partners, Inc., No. C 10-00010 JSW, 2011 WL 13153189, at *2 (N.D. Cal.
27
     Feb. 11, 2011) (“The expense of discovery alone does not amount to good cause to stay discovery
28


                                               6
                                 RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                          CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
            Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO              Document 30         Filed 09/30/25      Page 7 of 10



1
     based on Defendants’ argument that they are likely to succeed on the pending motions and could
2
     therefore avoid unnecessary expenses.”); see also Kor Media Grp., LLC v. Green, 294 F.R.D. 579,
3
     583 (D. Nev. 2013) (“The fact that discovery may involve inconvenience and expense is not
4
     sufficient, standing alone, to support a stay of discovery.”). That is precisely what United asserts
5
     here as the basis for its motion: “costly efforts to respond to discovery,” D.E. 28 at 7, and
6
     “substantial burden and expense[,]” D.E. 28 at 13. Concerns about cost and abstract invocations
7
     of “judicial efficiency,” D.E. 28 at 10, are insufficient. The true basis of this request is simply that
8
     United does not want the normal rules to apply.
9

10
             Even if this Court were to grant a motion to dismiss, Plaintiffs could still be entitled to

11   amend. Optronic Techs., Inc. v. Ningbo Sunny Elec. Co., No. 5:16-CV-06370-EJD, 2018 WL

12   1569811, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 16, 2018) (“[]Defendants correctly observe that the pending motion

13   to dismiss could be dispositive of the entire action, if granted in its entirety and if the court decides

14   that further leave to amend should not be permitted. But those are big ‘ifs.’”) (emphasis in

15   original); Singh v. Google, Inc., No. 16-CV-03734-BLF, 2016 WL 10807598, at *2 (N.D. Cal.
16   Nov. 4, 2016) (“Thus, even if Defendant were correct that Plaintiff’s claims must be dismissed as
17   alleged, the Court would consider whether leave to amend should be granted, rendering Google’s
18   motion not dispositive.”). In a case with a large number of different alternative remedies at issue,
19   Plaintiffs could easily end up repleading certain claims once the Court sets the law of the case.
20           Ultimately, “[i]dle speculation does not satisfy Rule 26(c)’s good cause requirement. Such
21
     general arguments could be said to apply to any reasonably large civil litigation.” Gray, 133 F.R.D.
22
     at 40. United offers a laundry list of cases in this District that it claims demonstrate that courts
23
     frequently grant motions to stay discovery. D.E. 28 at 9. But its citations are a thin reed. For
24
     example, United points to Joseph v. Koh, No. 20-CV-03782-WHO, 2020 WL 5824491, at *3 (N.D.
25
     Cal. Oct. 1, 2020), decided by this Court. But in that opinion, this Court also concurrently granted
26
     a motion to dismiss. That has not yet happened here, making the Koh opinion inapposite. And
27
     several of the cases United cites are antitrust cases, where the Supreme Court has articulated more
28


                                                7
                                  RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO UWM’S MOT. TO STAY DISC.
                                                           CASE NO. 3:25-CV 05377-WHO
            Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO             Document 30        Filed 09/30/25       Page 8 of 10



1
     specific rules regarding stays of discovery. In re Google Digital Advert. Antitrust Litig., No. 20-
2
     CV-03556-BLF, 2020 WL 7227159, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 8, 2020); Reveal Chat Holdco, LLC v.
3
     Facebook, Inc., No. 20-CV-00363-BLF, 2020 WL 2843369, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 10, 2020).
4
     Ultimately, United fails on the first and most important prong of the test – its motion is not
5
     dispositive, and so no protective order may issue. Even if the Court found that the two prongs of
6
     the test were satisfied, it can still (and should) decline to issue a protective order. Hoopes Vineyard
7
     LLC, 2025 WL 41929, at *1.
8
                                               CONCLUSION
9

10
            The instant Motion is a fairly typical request where a big company simply does not want

11   to engage in discovery, trumpets that its Motion to Dismiss will be the fairest Motion to Dismiss

12   of all, and points to no real burden other than the cost of discovery. It should be denied.

13

 1   I.     INTRODUCTION

 2          United Wholesale Mortgage, LLC (“UWM”) requests that the Court consider the

 3   following documents in connection with UWM’s motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) because

 4   each item is subject to judicial notice under Federal Rule of Evidence 201 and because they are

 5   incorporated by reference into Plaintiffs’ Amended Complaint (“AC”):

 6          •   Exhibit A of the AC: UWM’s Terms of Use, also available at

 7              https://www.uwm.com/terms-of-use (last visited August 22, 2025)

 8          •   Exhibit B of the AC: UWM’s Privacy Policy, also available at

 9              https://www.uwm.com/privacy-policy (last visited August 22, 2025)

10          •   Exhibit 1 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: Homepage of the UWM Website,

11              available at https://www.uwm.com/ (last visited August 19, 2025)

12          •   Exhibit 2 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: UWM Website’s “Mortgage

13              Loan Servicing” directory, available at https://uwm.com/loan-servicing (last visited

14              August 19, 2025)

15          •   Exhibit 3 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: UWM Website’s Cookie Banner,

16              available at https://www.uwm.com/ (last visited August 19, 2025)

17          •   Exhibit 4 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: Meta’s Terms of Service,

18              available at https://www.facebook.com/legal/terms (last visited August 19, 2025)

19          •   Exhibit 5 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: Meta’s Privacy Policy, available

20              at https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy (last visited August 19, 2025)

21          •   Exhibit 6 of the Declaration of Randall W. Edwards: Meta’s Cookies Policy, available

22              at https://www.facebook.com/policies/cookies/ (last visited August 19, 2025)

23          The principles of judicial notice and incorporation by reference allow consideration of

24   these documents because the documents are not subject to reasonable dispute, are core to

25   Plaintiff’s claims, and are either attached to or expressly referenced in Plaintiffs’ AC. They also

26   are readily accessible to the public. In addition, as the governing agreements, the words in these

27   documents are legally operative acts, not hearsay. See United States v. Pang, 362 F.3d 1187,

28   1192 (9th Cir. 2004).
                                                                                            UWM RJN ISO
                                                     1                                 MOT. TO. DISMISS
                                                                                  NO. 3:25-CV-05377-WHO
      Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO           Document 29-1        Filed 09/26/25      Page 3 of 6



 1          Some courts treat the incorporation by reference doctrine as part of judicial notice, while

 2   others treat them as distinct. Terraza v. Safeway Inc., 241 F. Supp. 3d 1057, 1067 (N.D. Cal.

 3   2017). Either way, however, both doctrines apply here.

 4   II.    ARGUMENT
 5          A court may “consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint,

 6   documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without

 7   converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment.” Herguan Univ. v.

 8   Immigr. & Customs Enf't, 258 F. Supp. 3d 1050, 1064 (N.D. Cal. 2017) (quoting United States v.

 9   Ritchie, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003)). The Court may deem documents incorporated by

10   reference where the AC attaches or refers to these documents, and they form the basis for

11   Plaintiffs’ claims. Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A., 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012) (A court

12   may consider “documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no

13   party questions, but which are not physically attached to the plaintiff’s pleading,” and “treat such

14   documents as part of the complaint”) (citing Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th

15   Cir.2005); Ritchie, 342 F.3d at 908.). And when a court deems a document incorporated by

16   reference, it may assume its contents are true for the purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule

17   12(b)(6). Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 1003 (9th Cir. 2018).

18          Here, Exhibits A and B, UWM’s Terms of Use and Privacy Policy, respectively, are

19   attached to the AC. E.g., In re Sorrento Therapeutics, 2021 WL 6062943, at *4 (incorporating by

20   reference document quoted from and referenced in complaint).

21          The Court also may deem Exhibits 1-6 of the Edwards Declaration incorporated by

22   reference because those documents show contents from websites that are expressly and implicitly

23   referenced in the AC. UWM’s Website and Cookies Banner, and Meta Platforms, Inc.

24   (“Facebook” or “Meta”)’s Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Cookies Policy are incorporated

25   by reference because Plaintiffs’ AC is based on and extensively references the UWM Website

26   and the Meta Pixel, as well as their alleged collection and sharing of Plaintiffs’ information.

27   Plaintiffs reference and quote UWM’s website throughout the AC. See AC. ¶¶ 2-4, 6, 13-14, 25

28   n.5, 28-30, 33-42, 45, 52-54, 57-70, 83, 102, 108, 110-121, 128, 133, 156, 161, 172, 175-176,
                                                                                            UWM RJN ISO
                                                      2                                MOT. TO. DISMISS
                                                                                  NO. 3:25-CV-05377-WHO
      Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO             Document 29-1         Filed 09/26/25   Page 4 of 6



 1   186-187, 233, 236-237, 253, 265-269, 283-287, 297, 300, 306-311, 324-325. Plaintiffs also state

 2   in the AC that they are “Facebook user[s],” id. ¶¶ 112, 118, and discuss extensively how

 3   “Plaintiffs’ interactions with UWM’s [website] were disclosed to third parties, including

 4   Facebook.” Id. ¶ 127, see id. ¶¶ 12, 31, 40-44, 56, 63, 90, 127, 128(f), 175, 198, 261(j), 279(t)

 5   329. As Facebook users, Plaintiffs must have accepted Meta’s Terms and Conditions, Privacy

 6   Policy, and Cookie Policy when they accessed UWM’s website. See id. ¶¶ 112, 118. Moreover,

 7   Plaintiffs’ claims are based on UWM’s purported sharing of information pertaining to themselves

 8   and other putative class members, and are predicated on the allegation that personal and financial

 9   information that they conveyed while accessing UWM’s website was collected by pixel tracking

10   technology and shared with third parties without their consent. A key issue is what Plaintiffs (and

11   proposed class members) were told by UWM and by the third parties that allegedly intercepted

12   their information, and what terms they agreed to. Thus, the incorporation by reference document

13   applies to these documents, too. See In re Google Assistant Privacy Litig., 457 F. Supp. 3d 797,

14   813–14 (incorporating by reference Google’s Terms of Service and Privacy Policy where these

15   documents “form[ed] the basis” for Plaintiffs’ claims); Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights,

16   Ltd., 551 U.S. 308, 322 (2007) (on Rule 12(b)(6) motion, courts “must consider … documents

17   incorporated into the complaint by reference, and matters on which a court may take judicial

18   notice”); Knievel, 393 F.3d at 1076 (court may consider extrinsic document if “plaintiff’s claim

19   depends on the contents of [the] document”); Hoey v. Sony Elecs. Inc., 515 F. Supp. 2d 1099,

20   1103 (N.D. Cal. 2007) (court may take judicial notice of document if the complaint refers

21   extensively to it or if it forms the basis of plaintiffs’ claims).

22           Incorporation by reference also is appropriate here because it fulfills the purpose of the

23   doctrine, namely, to prevent Plaintiffs from highlighting only the portions of the UWM Website

24   and information about Facebook that support their claims while omitting the portions of those

25   same documents that weaken their claims. McCoy v. Alphabet, Inc., 2021 WL 405816, at *2

26   (N.D. Cal. Feb. 2, 2021) (“The doctrine prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of

27   documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that

28   weaken—or doom—their claims.”) (citing Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1002).
                                                                                             UWM RJN ISO
                                                        3                               MOT. TO. DISMISS
                                                                                   NO. 3:25-CV-05377-WHO
      Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO            Document 29-1         Filed 09/26/25       Page 5 of 6



 1           Independently, the Court may also take judicial notice of all the documents. Federal Rule

 2   of Evidence 201 permits a court to take judicial notice of a fact “not subject to reasonable

 3   dispute” because the fact is either “(1) [] generally known within the trial court’s territorial

 4   jurisdiction; or (2) can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot

 5   reasonably be questioned.” Fed. R. Evid. 201(b). Under Rule 201, “documents whose contents

 6   are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically

 7   attached to the pleading” may be considered in ruling on a 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss. Davis v.

 8   HSBC Bank Nev., N.A., 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012).

 9           Exhibits A & B to the AC and Exhibits 1-6 to the Edwards Declaration are publicly

10   available documents available on UWM’s and Meta’s webpages. Courts have regularly taken

11   notice of these types of documents previously. See, e.g., Opperman v. Path, Inc., 84 F. Supp. 3d

12   962, 976 (N.D. Cal. 2015) (taking judicial notice of Privacy Policy); Rutter v. Apple Inc., 2022

13   WL 1443336, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2022) (granting request for judicial notice of Terms and

14   Conditions); Jones v. Tonal Sys., Inc., 751 F. Supp. 3d 1025, 1031-32 (S.D. Cal. 2024) (judicial

15   notice of website); Loomis v. Slendertone Distribution, Inc., 420 F. Supp. 3d 1046, 1063 (S.D.

16   Cal. 2019) (same); Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1002-03 (a court may take notice of an adjudicative fact

17   not subject to reasonable dispute); In re Google Assistant Privacy Litig., 457 F. Supp. 3d 797,

18   813–14 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (taking judicial notice of company’s terms and conditions and privacy

19   policy); Caldwell v. Caldwell, 2006 WL 618511, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 13, 2006), order clarified,

20   2006 WL 734405 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 20, 2006) (“[A]s a general matter, websites and their contents

21   may be proper subjects for judicial notice.”); Calhoun v. Google LLC, 526 F. Supp. 3d 605, 617

22   (N.D. Cal. 2021) (collecting cases holding that “documents [that] appear on publicly available

23   websites. . . are . . . proper subjects for judicial notice”); Minkler v. Apple, Inc., 65 F. Supp. 3d

24   810, 814 n.1 (N.D. Cal. 2014) (taking judicial notice of “Hardware Warranty . . . because [its]

25   accuracy is not disputed and [it is] referenced in the Complaint”); Doron Precision Sys., Inc. v.

26   FAAC, Inc., 423 F. Supp. 2d 173, 179 n.8 (S.D.N.Y. 2006) (“For purposes of a 12(b)(6) motion to

27   dismiss, a court may take judicial notice of information publicly announced on a party’s website,

28

                                                                                     NO. 3:25-CV-05377-WHO
      Case 3:25-cv-05377-WHO           Document 29-1          Filed 09/26/25    Page 6 of 6



 1   as long as the website’s authenticity is not in dispute and ‘it is capable of accurate and ready

 2   determination.’”) (quoting Fed. R. Evid. 201).

 3   III.   CONCLUSION

 4          For these reasons, UWM requests that the Court grant its request for consideration of

 5   Exhibits A-B of the AC and Exhibits 1-6 of the Edwards Declaration under the doctrines of

 6   incorporation by reference and judicial notice.
